title: Deterministic k-server conjecture
formal: For every integer \(k\ge1\), every finite or infinite metric space \((M,d)\) with at least \(k+1\) points, and every initial configuration \(C_0\in M^k\), do there exist a deterministic online rule \(A\) and a finite \(\beta\ge0\) such that \[\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma;C_0)\le k\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\] for every finite request sequence \(\sigma\)? Both parties have exactly \(k\) servers and start at \(C_0\); movement cost is the sum of distances in the model below. The rule and additive constant may depend on the metric and initial placement, but not on the future requests.
definitions:
For every integer \(k\ge1\), define the universal deterministic competitive-ratio infimum
\[R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=\inf\mathcal R_k,\]
where
\[\mathcal R_k=\Bigl\{r\in[1,\infty):\ \forall(M,d)\in\mathcal M_k\ \forall C_0\in M^k\ \exists A\ \exists\beta\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}\ \forall\sigma\in M^{<\omega},\quad
\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma;C_0)\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)+\beta\Bigr\}.\]
Here \(\mathcal M_k\) consists of all finite or infinite metric spaces having at least \(k+1\) points, \(A\) is a deterministic online rule in the serving model below, and \(M^{<\omega}\) is the set of all finite request sequences, including the empty sequence. 

A metric space here consists of a set \(M\) and a function \(d:M\times M\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\) with finite values, satisfying \(d(x,y)=0\) exactly when \(x=y\), symmetry, and \(d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)\). The space is known to the rule. It need not be finite, bounded, discrete, complete, compact, or given by computable distances. The quantifier ranges over ordinary set-based metric spaces.

There are exactly \(k\) servers with equal movement costs. For precise bookkeeping label them by \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and write a configuration as a tuple \(C=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\in M^k\). Several servers may occupy the same point. Labels only identify which server moves and confer no different costs or service capabilities; the physical configuration is a multiset. The initial tuple \(C_0\) is specified before the first request and is identical for the online rule and the offline comparator.

For a request sequence \(\sigma=(q_1,\ldots,q_T)\), request \(q_t\) must be served before \(q_{t+1}\) is revealed. If a server already occupies \(q_t\), all servers stay put and the cost of that step is zero. Otherwise the rule chooses one index \(i_t\in[k]\), moves that server from its current position \(x_{i_t,t-1}\) to \(q_t\), and pays \(d(x_{i_t,t-1},q_t)\). All other positions remain unchanged. Let \(\delta_t\) denote this step cost. The total cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\delta_t\). These are lazy moves; for the ordinary sum-of-movement-distances objective, the classical laziness lemma shows that this restriction does not worsen the attainable competitive guarantees.

A deterministic online rule is a function assigning a legal next move to each nonempty revealed request prefix, with the current configuration determined recursively from earlier moves. On two sequences with the same prefix it must make the same decisions through that prefix. It may use the known metric, \(k\), the initial tuple, and the whole revealed history. No random bits, future-dependent advice, request horizon or next request are provided. All finite sequences are included, of arbitrary length; the definition also covers requests chosen adaptively from the rule's past moves. Covered requests may remain in the remembered history.

This is a question about existence of online decision rules, without any time, space, computability, finite-program or finite-precision restriction. In particular, a rule on a specified real metric is an abstract function; no unmentioned representation of all real distances is required. The ratio \(r\) depends only on \(k\). The chosen rule and finite constant \(\beta\) may depend on \(k,r,(M,d),C_0\), but neither may be chosen after seeing the future sequence. The same \(A,\beta\) must satisfy the inequality for all sequence lengths and contents on that metric and initial placement.

The quantity \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma;C_0)\) is the minimum total cost of all legal lazy move sequences serving \(\sigma\) from \(C_0\), with all requests known in advance. There are at most \(k^T\) choices of server indices, so the minimum is attained and finite even when \(M\) is infinite. Both costs are zero for the empty sequence. There is no final return requirement and no prescribed terminal configuration. The competitive inequality is used directly, including when \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\); it is not a quotient by a possibly zero cost.

Movement costs and \(\beta\) have the same distance units, while \(r\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\) are dimensionless. Multiplying all distances by a positive constant rescales costs and the allowed additive constant, but does not change the competitive ratio. No normalization of metric diameter is imposed.

The known universal upper bound gives \(2k-1\in\mathcal R_k\), so this set is nonempty and its real infimum exists; the deterministic lower bound gives \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The infimum need not be attained. For \(u\ge1\), an upper bound \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le u\) means that for every \(\eta>0\), the ratio \(u+\eta\) belongs to \(\mathcal R_k\). The selected rules and additive constants may depend on \(\eta\). A lower bound \(\ell\ge1\) means that for every \(r\in[1,\ell)\) there exist a metric and initial placement such that every online rule and every finite additive constant fail the competitive inequality on some finite sequence. The obstructing metric may depend on \(r\); no single metric witnessing attainment of a supremum is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the displayed assertion or of its logical negation, with exactly the stated model, quantifier order and parameter dependence. A bound for a restricted subclass or one particular algorithm is insufficient to refute a universal existence assertion. Determining the entire optimal rate or a numerical approximation to it is not required.
why: The k-server problem measures the movement cost of responding to demand without knowing future requests. It includes paging and serves as a basic problem in competitive analysis, with the same number of resources available to the online rule and the offline optimum.

progress.text: Manasse–McGeoch–Sleator establish the deterministic lower bound \(k\), the two-server case and the \((k+1)\)-point case.
Koutsoupias–Papadimitriou establish the general \(2k-1\) deterministic upper bound. The inspected author-hosted manuscript is dated 22 May 1995.
Huang–Zhang prove the three-server circle theorem; their canonical-certificate limitation has a separate restricted scope.
Bubeck–Coester–Rabani's preprint, published at STOC 2023, disproves the randomized logarithmic conjecture with a squared-logarithmic lower bound.
ISAAC publishes a \(2k-1\) lower bound for the time-optimal variant. Its maximum-movement objective differs from the classical sum-of-distances objective.
The potential-discovery benchmark retains the general deterministic conjecture and records the limits of its finite experiments.
ICALP publishes polynomial-time randomized algorithms and a separate advice-assisted consequence, retaining their additional randomness or input.

A new preprint claims that the work-function algorithm is \(k\)-competitive on every metric, with an explicit sequence-independent additive term. If correct, its Theorem 1.2 and the classical lower bound determine \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\) exactly. The claim is not independently verified here.

status_note: Matching claimed resolution found on 16 September 2026: Coester–Koutsoupias–Zbysiński, arXiv:2609.15979v1, submitted 14 September, Theorem 1.2 states WFA cost at most k times OPT plus the pairwise-distance sum of the initial configuration on every metric and finite sequence. Its scope covers the retained model, including repeated initial locations via distinct labels. Combined with the established lower bound, the claimed theorem would give R_det(k)=k for every k and establish the binary k-competitiveness assertion selected here. The full PDF, model, theorem and proof organization were inspected, but the complete proof is not independently certified or Lean-checked here. Status is uncertain pending verification, superseding the previous source-open assessment.

context_blocks.text: On the uniform metric, where every two different points have distance one, the covered points represent pages currently in a cache. A request at an uncovered point incurs a page replacement. General metrics permit different movement costs between different demand locations. The comparison here always gives exactly \(k\) servers to both parties.

Manasse, McGeoch and Sleator prove the deterministic lower bound \(k\) and a matching algorithm for two servers. Their original paper also handles metrics with exactly \(k+1\) points. The lower-bound argument permits an offline starting-position change at a finite additive cost, so requiring the same initial placement does not remove the asymptotic obstruction. Together with the direct one-server case, the established initial values are \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(1)=1\) and \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(2)=2\).

Koutsoupias and Papadimitriou establish a universal \((2k-1)\)-competitive deterministic rule, the work-function algorithm. Their manuscript explicitly allows infinite metrics and repeated server locations. As the classical bound before the September 2026 claim, this yields \(k\le R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)\le2k-1\). The result concerns competitive movement cost; it does not supply a polynomial running-time guarantee, and the present target does not require one.

The selected target is the classical conjecture asserting an actual \(k\)-competitive rule. It implies \(R_{\mathrm{det}}(k)=k\), but an infimum value alone need not give endpoint attainment. The September 2026 preprint claims the actual competitiveness statement; its proof-review caveat is retained below.

Chrobak and Larmore obtain the optimal factor \(k\) on tree metrics, whose distances are the lengths of unique connecting paths in an edge-weighted tree. This covers the line as a special case. It is a guarantee for that geometry rather than for every metric.

Huang and Zhang prove that the work-function algorithm is 3-competitive on a circle. For circumference \(L>0\), this metric is \([0,L)\) with \(d(x,y)=\min\{|x-y|,L-|x-y|\}\). Their separate computer-assisted limitation concerns a precisely defined family of potential certificates under a specified universal condition. It does not disprove 3-competitiveness of all online rules or exclude every proof for the work-function algorithm. The inspected text is the 2022 preprint; the journal article appeared in 2024.

Bubeck, Coester and Rabani give metrics on \(k+1\) points with randomized competitive ratio \(\Omega(\log^2 k)\). This refutes the randomized \(O(\log k)\) conjecture. Their ratio compares expected movement cost to the offline optimum with a sequence-independent additive constant. It neither refutes the deterministic factor \(k\) nor determines the deterministic infimum function.

Frei and coauthors' ISAAC 2025 result has a deterministic lower bound \(2k-1\) for a different objective: each request costs the maximum simultaneous server movement, rather than the sum of movements. That time objective can reward moving several servers at once, so the lazy distance model in this card is not an interchangeable formulation. The new lower bound is not a matching lower bound for \(R_{\mathrm{det}}\).

The April 2026 k-server-bench preprint evaluates candidate proof certificates on finite instances, including four-server circle instances. It explicitly distinguishes passing those finite checks from a proof covering all configurations and request sequences. Its reported experiments do not resolve the remaining general case.

Coester and Cosson's ICALP 2026 theorem gives a polynomial-time randomized \(O(\log n\log^2 k)\)-competitive algorithm on \(n\)-point metrics. Its reduction uses few random bits, but does not eliminate randomness. A separate deterministic consequence supplies advice that depends on the instance. Neither extra input nor randomization is present in this card, so these computational improvements do not determine its universal deterministic ratio.

Coester, Koutsoupias and Zbysiński's preprint submitted on 14 September 2026 states in Theorem 1.2 that, for every metric and every finite request sequence,
\[\operatorname{WFA}_{C_0}(\sigma)\le k\operatorname{OPT}_{C_0}(\sigma)+\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}d(s_i,s_j).\]
Here \(s_1,\ldots,s_k\) are the initial server locations. The additive term is finite and depends only on the initial placement, as permitted here. The paper explicitly handles coincident positions with distinct location labels and a pseudometric, and states the theorem for any metric space. Its lazy implementation agrees with the serving convention of this card. The matching claim changes the current status to uncertain pending verification; this review has not independently certified the whole proof.

sentences: The k-server problem serves successive requests by moving one of k servers in a known metric.
The online rule sees only requests that have already arrived.
The conjecture asks for cost at most k times the offline optimum plus a fixed additive constant.
It permits unrestricted computation and both finite and infinite metric spaces.
A ratio approaching k without an actual k-competitive rule does not establish the selected assertion.
